terms.definition: A website made of pre-built HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and image files that are served identically to every visitor — no backend logic required.
terms.example: A school brochure website with fixed pages — like a printed flyer that is the same for everyone.

terms.definition: A website that generates pages on the fly using server-side code (Node.js, Python, PHP, etc.) and databases. Content varies per user or session.
terms.example: Your Amazon shopping cart page — it shows your specific items, not the same page for everyone.

terms.definition: An Amazon S3 feature that allows you to serve a static website directly from a bucket. No EC2, no Apache, no server management required.
terms.example: Upload index.html and CSS to an S3 bucket, enable this feature, and get a website endpoint URL.

terms.definition: The filename of the main landing page that S3 serves when a user visits the root website URL. Must match the actual filename exactly.
terms.example: index.html — the most common index document name for static websites.

terms.definition: An S3 bucket-level setting that prevents public access permissions from being applied. Must be disabled before a bucket policy can make the bucket public.
terms.example: Like a master lock on a safe — even if you write a permission rule, it won't work until the master lock is unlocked.

terms.definition: A JSON document attached to an S3 bucket that defines who can access the bucket and what actions they can perform. Controls access via Effect, Principal, Action, and Resource.
terms.example: A policy with Principal * and Action s3:GetObject makes all objects in the bucket publicly readable.

terms.definition: Content Delivery Network — a globally distributed network of servers (edge locations) that caches content near users to deliver it faster and reduce latency.
terms.example: Like opening pizza delivery branches near your customers instead of delivering from one central kitchen.

terms.definition: The time delay between a user sending a request and receiving the response. High latency means slow response; low latency means fast response.
terms.example: A user in Germany accessing a server in Mumbai has high latency — the data travels thousands of kilometers.

terms.definition: A mini data center in the CDN network that caches content close to users. Also called a Point of Presence (PoP). Different from AWS Regions and Availability Zones.
terms.example: A CloudFront edge location in Frankfurt serves cached content to European users — they don't need to contact Mumbai.

terms.definition: Another name for a CDN edge location — a mini data center strategically placed to serve users from a nearby geographic location.
terms.example: AWS has hundreds of PoPs globally, ensuring users always have a nearby edge location to connect to.

terms.definition: The primary source where your actual content lives — the bucket or server from which CDN edge locations fetch content for caching.
terms.example: Your S3 bucket in Mumbai is the origin. Edge locations in Germany fetch from it and cache locally.

terms.definition: AWS managed Content Delivery Network (CDN) service. Delivers content with low latency and high transfer speeds via a global network of edge locations.
terms.example: A CloudFront distribution in front of an S3 bucket reduces load times for global users from seconds to milliseconds.

terms.definition: The CloudFront configuration that defines your CDN setup — what the origin is, what root document to serve, caching settings, and security options.
terms.example: You create one distribution per website, specifying S3 as the origin and index.html as the root document.

terms.definition: A CDN scenario where the requested content is already stored at the edge location — served instantly without contacting the origin server.
terms.example: The second user from Germany requesting the same page gets a cache hit — served from Frankfurt instantly.

terms.definition: A CDN scenario where the requested content is not yet cached at the edge location — it must be fetched from the origin server first.
terms.example: The first user from Germany requesting a file triggers a cache miss — edge fetches from Mumbai, caches it, then serves.

terms.definition: The duration (in seconds) that a CDN edge location keeps a cached copy of content before refreshing from the origin. Balances freshness vs. caching efficiency.
terms.example: TTL of 300 seconds means edge locations refresh from S3 every 5 minutes — useful for frequently updated content.

terms.definition: A CloudFront operation that forces edge locations to discard their cached copies and fetch fresh content from the origin on the next request.
terms.example: After updating website files in S3, you create an invalidation for /* to force all edge locations to serve the new version immediately.

terms.definition: A CloudFront security feature that grants a specific CloudFront distribution exclusive access to a private S3 bucket, without making the bucket public.
terms.example: Like giving a key only to your delivery driver — CloudFront gets the key (OAC), but the general public cannot open the door (private bucket).

terms.definition: The legacy predecessor to OAC for restricting CloudFront access to private S3 buckets. AWS now recommends OAC over OAI for new distributions.
terms.example: Old distributions may use OAI — if migrating, switch to OAC for better security including SSE-KMS support.

terms.definition: The CloudFront setting that specifies which file to serve when a user visits the root URL of a CloudFront distribution (e.g., index.html).
terms.example: Without this, visiting xyz.cloudfront.net shows an error. With it set to index.html, your homepage loads.

terms.definition: The entity (who) that a bucket policy applies to. Can be everyone (*), a specific AWS service (cloudfront.amazonaws.com), an IAM user, or an IAM role.
terms.example: In a public bucket policy, Principal * means the entire internet. In an OAC policy, Principal is cloudfront.amazonaws.com.

terms.definition: An HTTP error returned when a user tries to access a resource they don't have permission to read. Common in S3 when the bucket is private or bucket policy is missing.
terms.example: Accessing an S3 website URL before adding a public bucket policy returns 403 Forbidden.
